message.content: $50 keeps the pressure on p4’s cash cap without overpaying. I’ll take it at $75 if they stay in.
message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for Kentucky Avenue.

I have $1,179 in cash and no monopolies. The current bid is $49 from p4. I am in jail on turn 2 of 3. p4 has $74 and owns Park Place with one house and Boardwalk with two houses.

p3 and p1 have dropped out. p3 has $97 and owns all four railroads, a pink monopoly with houses, and Illinois Avenue. p1 has $15 and owns an orange monopoly with houses plus mortgaged properties.

My strategy is to raise the bid by one dollar each turn until p4 reaches their $74 cash limit. I will then take the property at $75. Winning prevents p4 from using a $110 emergency mortgage on dark-blue houses. I will not bid above $110.

I am weighing whether to bid $50 now or wait. p4 has been stubbornly matching every one-dollar increment, so they may keep bidding until their $74 cash limit. I suspect they want Kentucky for its $110 mortgage value, to deny me, or simply to be competitive.

I am weighing the cash cost of winning. I need $50 to exit jail on turn 3 and $320 for PA Avenue. p4 would be left with almost no cash buffer if they bid up to their limit.

Winning at $75 leaves me with about $734 after paying the $50 jail fee and $320 for PA Avenue. Even at $110, I would still have roughly $699. This buffer comfortably covers a potential hit on pinks or oranges.

Owning Kentucky also blocks p3 from completing their red set, since they already hold Illinois and p1 has Indiana mortgaged.

Bidding $75 now would win immediately, since p4 only has $74 and cannot afford the next increment. The risk is that they might drop out at a lower price if I keep min-raising, saving money. The trade-off is between paying $75 for sure versus potentially winning cheaper.

I will bid $50. Min-raising is the better strategy because it saves money if p4 drops out early, and it still wins at $75 if they reach their cash limit. There is no downside to more auction rounds.

If I drop out, p4 wins at $49 and keeps $25 cash. They gain $61 in mortgage liquidity and a rent chip. If I bid $50–75, I gain the same liquidity but deny it to them. This makes the auction worth fighting for.

p4's Boardwalk at two houses yields $600 in rent. Park Place with one house yields $175. That is a serious threat, but p4 cannot build more houses right now because each costs $200 and they only have $74.

Mortgaging Kentucky would not immediately let p4 build more houses. They would still need $200 per house. Selling all three of their existing houses would raise only about $300, which is not enough to cover the cost of new houses plus the mortgage. The real danger is that p4 survives long enough to hit me with a $600 Boardwalk rent or build up to $1,400.
